studies.title: These Are The Signs
studies.meaning: Three statements in one line, and the last is the unexpected one. Detached letters open the surah, then the ayat are pointed at as the signs of the Book, then what has been sent down is called the truth. The closing clause does not defend that claim. It reports the response to it: most people do not believe. Placing the count at the outset takes the weight of numbers off everything that follows, and the surah never treats the fact as a difficulty afterwards.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as a Medinan revelation. Early scholars record disagreement about that, and some place it in Mecca. Its subject belongs to a long argument about signs, revelation and denial, not to any single incident. Early scholars report no occasion for this opening ayah. They read it as setting the terms for everything the surah goes on to say.

keyTerms.note: A demonstrative for something at a distance rather than close at hand. Pointing at the ayat with the far form gives them a standing above the speaker, which is why translators reach for a formal these.
The word covers truth in speech and reality in fact together. Calling revelation this says it corresponds to how things are, not merely that its statements are accurate about them.
A comparative used as a plain quantity. Its presence turns the closing clause into a count rather than a complaint, which is why the sentence reports the response instead of protesting against it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia measured a claim by who accepted it. A poet's standing, a family line, a treaty: all of them rested on broad agreement. A view held by a few was, in practice, wrong. Opening a text by granting that most people would not accept it cut against the way the culture settled questions. The first listeners would have felt that at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase pointing at the signs of the Book opens seven surahs of the Quran. All seven stand right after a set of disconnected letters. The formula never appears in the middle of an argument. It only comes at the head of a chapter. That makes it work rather like a title line placed above what follows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah separates the truth of a message from how it is received. It does so before any argument has begun. That has a practical effect on a reader. Nothing later in the surah has to explain away the number of people who disagree. It also makes the Book itself the thing being pointed at, so what follows is offered as evidence rather than as assertion.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same observation about numbers, in the surah immediately before this one.
Returns to the same division later in the surah, between one who knows and one who is blind.
Opens another surah with the identical phrase pointing at the signs of the Book.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much weight you give to how many people agree with you. It is usually more than you would admit if asked. Pick one thing you believe and hold it this week without checking whether it is popular. The ayah puts the count in its opening line precisely so that it stops working as an argument.
studies.explainEasier: The surah opens with letters, then points to its own verses. It says this book is the truth, sent down from your Lord. Then it says plainly that most people will not believe it.

studies.title: Pillars You Cannot See
studies.meaning: A sequence of acts, and most of them are still going on. The heavens are raised without pillars you can see, which early scholars read two ways: either there are none, or there are supports that are not visible. Sun and moon are set running to a fixed term. Then two verbs describe continuing work, directing the affair and setting out the signs, and the stated purpose of the whole line is certainty about a meeting. Cosmology is being used to make a point about an appointment.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, though early scholars record disagreement about it. Its opening section belongs to the Quran's long argument from natural order. It is addressed to people who accepted a creator while denying that the dead would be raised. That gap is what the ayah works on. The surah quotes the denial directly three ayat later.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for the poles of a tent or a building. Early scholars read the phrase either as meaning there are none at all or that the supports are not visible, and they preserve both readings.
The verb for putting something under command so that it serves a purpose, used of animals and of labourers. Applied to the sun and moon it describes them as employed rather than merely existing.
From a root meaning the back or the end of a thing. To direct an affair in Arabic is to consider what comes after it, so the word carries the sense of arranging with an outcome already in view.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tent was the most familiar structure in Arabia, and its whole logic was visible poles. Take out the centre pole and the roof comes down. Everyone had raised one and struck one. Saying that the sky stands without any pole you can see borrowed the most ordinary building knowledge in the culture. Then it removed the central assumption in five words.
studies.didYouKnow: This description of the heavens raised without visible pillars occurs twice in the Quran. It is here and at 31:10, in identical wording. Both are followed at once by a list of things placed in the earth. Both belong to passages arguing from what a person can see towards something they cannot.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah gives a reason for describing the cosmos, and the reason is not wonder. The stated purpose is certainty about meeting your Lord. The whole description aims at one conclusion about the future. That makes the argument tighter than it first looks. A thing running to a fixed term is a thing that ends. The ordering of the sky is offered as evidence that endings are arranged rather than accidental.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same description of the heavens in identical wording, in another argument from creation.
Uses the same phrase about the sun and moon each running to an appointed limit.
Extends the same idea of measure and appointment from the sky to the womb, later in the surah.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight and find the moon, then hold it against the fact that it is running to a term. Not as a poetic thought, but as a piece of information about a body you can actually see. The argument in this ayah only works if you look up, which takes about forty seconds.
studies.explainEasier: God raised the sky with no pillars you can see. He set the sun and moon running, each for a set time. He runs everything and shows the signs, so people may be sure they will meet him.

studies.title: Two Of Every Kind
studies.meaning: The scale drops from the sky to the ground, and the verbs change with it. The earth is spread out. Mountains and rivers are placed in it. Then something more precise arrives: two of every kind of fruit. Early scholars read the pairing as varieties, or as male and female in plants. The second reading matches what date growers already knew. The closing image is night drawing over day, and the sign is addressed to people who reflect.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about that. This section moves through a run of natural descriptions. Each one closes by naming a different faculty: reflection here, reasoning in the ayah after it. The audience assumed is one that already accepted a creator. So the argument is not about who made these things. It is about what follows from the way they are arranged.

keyTerms.note: The verb for stretching something flat, used of a cloth laid out and of a shadow lengthening. It describes an action still visible in its result rather than a single completed event in the past.
From the verb for a ship dropping anchor and holding its position. Mountains are named by their function of holding rather than by their height, which is how the Quran refers to them throughout.
A form of the verb to think that implies turning something repeatedly in the mind. It is slower than reasoning, and the surah asks for a different faculty in each of these consecutive ayat.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date growers in Arabia had known for centuries that palms come as male and female. A crop depends on carrying pollen from one to the other by hand. It was skilled seasonal work, and everyone in an oasis understood it. Naming pairs in fruit spoke straight into that knowledge. The survival of a settlement rested on getting it right.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for two of a kind used here occurs three times in the Quran. Once of the pairs taken aboard the ark at 11:40, once in the retelling of the same event at 23:27, and once here of fruit. One expression covers animals preserved from a flood and the varieties growing in an orchard.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah asks for reflection rather than agreement, and reflection is the slower of the two. What is put in front of it is not a marvel but an arrangement. Things placed, held, paired and alternated. That points to a particular kind of argument, one that works by piling up rather than by a single decisive proof. It explains why the surah keeps to ordinary features of the world.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same list and asks for a different faculty at its close, reasoning rather than reflection.
States the pairing of created things as a general principle rather than only about fruit.
Follows the same movement from night drawing over day to the sun and moon running their courses.

studies.applyIt: Eat one piece of fruit slowly this week and stay with it for the whole of it. Where it grew, who moved the pollen, how the water reached it. The faculty this ayah asks for is not admiration. It is the turning over of something you already have in your hand, and it takes about two minutes.
studies.explainEasier: God spread out the earth. He put mountains and rivers in it, and made two of every kind of fruit. He draws night over day. There are signs in this for people who think.

studies.title: Watered By The Same Water
studies.meaning: The argument narrows to a single field. Neighbouring plots, vines, crops and palms. Some grow from one root and some from separate roots. All are fed by one water, and the yields differ. The interest lies entirely in the constant: the water is the same. Early scholars read the ayah as an argument about different results from identical inputs. They note that it is addressed to people who reason, since the point has to be drawn out rather than simply looked at.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about it. Farming in the oases and around Medina was intensely local. Plots of different quality lay side by side and drew from the same channel. The ayah describes a scene any listener could walk out and check. It closes a run of natural descriptions with the plainest of them.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a neighbour, used elsewhere in the Quran of people. Applying it to plots of ground makes them neighbours to one another, which keeps the whole comparison close and physical.
A technical term from date farming for palms sharing a single root, occurring only in this ayah. Its opposite follows immediately, so both cases are named inside four words.
The noun for what a tree produces to be eaten, rather than for the tree itself. Preferring one over another in yield is therefore a statement about the crop and not about the plant's worth.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Irrigation in an oasis was shared and timed. Water ran through channels and each holder took a turn measured by the sun or by a marked stone, and disputes over turns were common enough to need arbitration. Everyone therefore knew with certainty that the water in their plot and their neighbour's was the same water. This ayah is built on that certainty.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for palms sharing a single root occurs only in this ayah in the whole Quran. Its own opposite follows in the next three words. It is a term from the working vocabulary of date farming. It is used with no explanation at all. That assumes a listener who has handled the trees himself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah sets up a controlled comparison and leaves the conclusion to the reader. Same input, next-door ground, different results, and the difference is given directly to God. The application to people is obvious and is not spelled out here. The surah returns to it later, with the image of a flood filling riverbeds of different size. Difference is presented as designed, not as accident and not as merit.

crossReferences.why: Draws the same conclusion about differing capacities, using water and a flood as its image.
Lists similar produce and makes the same point about likeness and difference in one clause.
Extends the same observation about variety from crops to rock and to living creatures.

studies.applyIt: Think of two people you know who were given much the same start and turned out differently. Resist the ranking your mind will immediately offer. This ayah names the difference and attributes it without ever saying which crop was the better plant. Try holding one such comparison for a day with no verdict attached.
studies.explainEasier: In one field there are plots side by side with vines, crops and palm trees. The same water feeds all of them. Yet some give better fruit than others. God makes them different.

studies.title: The Real Astonishment
studies.meaning: This is a response to a reaction. If anything is going to strike you as strange, the passage says, the strange thing is the sentence they keep saying. They ask whether, once they are dust, they will be a new creation. What is called astonishing is not the raising but the objection to it. That reversal is the whole argument. Three parallel clauses follow, each opening the same way. The middle one gives an image of collars at the neck, which early scholars read as present and as coming.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among early scholars. The denial quoted here appears many times across the Quran, nearly always in the same words. That suggests a standard objection rather than a single occasion. The argument around it in this surah rests on the natural order just described. Being raised is presented as continuous with what a person can already see.

keyTerms.note: The verb for finding something outside expectation. The ayah uses the root twice in one clause, once conditionally of the listener and once of the objection itself, which is what performs the reversal.
The ordinary word for the earth underfoot. The objection depends on it being the least promising material imaginable, and the Quran elsewhere makes the same word the origin of the first human being.
Iron rings fastened at the neck, used on prisoners and on animals. Early scholars divide over the tense, reading them as a coming condition or as a present restriction on how a person can turn.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burial in Arabia was quick and shallow, and in that heat and soil a body returned to the ground within a season. People did not meet death at a distance. They carried it, washed it and covered it themselves, often within a day. The objection quoted here was not abstract philosophy. It came from people who had recently handled what they were describing.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase about collars on their necks occurs only in this ayah. The image of a collar does return elsewhere in the Quran. Early scholars divide over its tense. Some read it as a description of what is coming. Others read it as a statement about how such a person already moves, unable to turn the head.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah moves where the strangeness sits. Anyone meeting a claim about the dead being raised will treat that as the odd item. The passage answers that the odd item is the denial, given what has just been said about the arrangement of the world. That is an argument about consistency rather than about evidence. It rests entirely on the four ayat before it.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the description of ordered creation on which this ayah's reversal depends.
Answers the same objection about bones and dust with an argument from first creation.
Quotes the same objection in almost the same words, and calls the distance imagined a mistake.

studies.applyIt: Notice which claims strike you as obviously strange and which pass without any comment at all. The sorting is mostly habit rather than judgement. Take one thing you find hard to believe and one thing you accept without thinking, and set them honestly beside each other for five minutes. That comparison is the whole move this ayah makes.
studies.explainEasier: Some people say it is strange that God could raise them after they turn to dust. The ayah says the strange part is that they say it at all, after all the signs they have seen.

studies.title: Hurrying The Wrong Thing
studies.meaning: A strange request is reported. They want the bad brought forward ahead of the good. Early scholars read it as a demand for the punishment they had been warned about, made to test the warning. The reply notes that examples of exactly that have already passed by. Then two statements about God are set side by side and never reconciled. One is about forgiveness extended to people despite their wrongdoing. The other is about severity. The surah leaves them both standing.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with early scholars recording disagreement. The demand described here appears in several places in the Quran. It always comes from people confident that nothing would happen. It is always answered by pointing at earlier cases rather than by producing what was asked for. The examples referred to are ruined communities whose sites travellers passed on the trade routes.

keyTerms.gloss: and they ask you to hurry
keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to hasten meaning to ask somebody else to bring a thing forward. The request is addressed to a man who could not have granted it, which is part of what makes it a taunt.
A rare plural from the root for a likeness or a parable, occurring only here. It names punishments that became examples, so the word holds both the event and its later use as a lesson.

The preposition here means in spite of rather than because of. That small word is what makes the clause remarkable, since forgiveness is described as extended over the wrongdoing rather than after it stops.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The caravan routes north from Mecca passed the remains of settlements that had been abandoned or destroyed. The stories attached to them were common property. Travellers pointed them out to each other on the road. When this ayah says examples have already passed, it means places its first listeners had ridden past. It does not mean a literature they would have had to consult.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for exemplary punishments occurs only in this ayah. It is found nowhere else in the Quran. It is a plural from the same root that gives the word for a parable. So the Arabic treats a ruined town and a spoken likeness as two forms of one thing. Each is set up so that people will look at it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah places two divine attributes in one sentence without ranking them, and it puts forgiveness first. What makes the phrasing striking is that forgiveness is described as extended in spite of ongoing wrongdoing, not after repentance. That is not the usual order. The severity that follows is not withdrawn either. A reader is left holding both, which is where the surah wants them.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same subject later in the surah: respite given, and then a seizure.
Reports the same demand and answers it by naming communities given respite before them.
Sets the same two statements side by side, in the same order, without resolving them either.

studies.applyIt: Notice the times you would rather have the bad news now than wait. It usually feels like courage and is often impatience with uncertainty. Before you force a difficult thing forward this week, ask what the waiting is actually for. This ayah puts forgiveness inside exactly that interval, before anything has been settled.
studies.explainEasier: Some people dared God to send the punishment early. The ayah says such things have already happened to other towns. God forgives people even while they do wrong. He can also punish hard.

studies.title: To Every People A Guide
studies.meaning: A demand for a sign is quoted and answered in two short clauses, and neither of them is a defence. The first defines the office: you are only a warner. The second widens the frame considerably, saying that every community has a guide. Early scholars divide over that second clause, reading the guide as God, or as a messenger sent to each people, or as anyone who calls to the truth. The demand for a miracle is left unanswered on its own terms.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded. The demand quoted here is repeated word for word later in the same surah at 13:27, and answered differently there. Early scholars note that. The Quran reports this request in several places and consistently declines to meet it. It redirects instead to the message itself, or to signs already available in the ordinary world.

keyTerms.note: A particle of urging that can carry either a complaint or a wish. Used with a passive verb it makes the objection sound like a reasonable request, which is exactly how it works in the mouths quoted here.

An agent noun from the verb to warn of something coming. The restriction placed in front of it narrows the office deliberately: not a producer of signs and not a judge, but somebody who tells you what is ahead.
From the verb to lead along a road. The indefinite form leaves the identity open, which is why the classical readings differ over whether it names God, a messenger, or anyone who points the way.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A guide was a paid professional in Arabia. Crossing open desert without one was reckless, and a good guide could read stars, stones and wind-shaped sand to hold a party on a route with no visible track. Communities knew who theirs was. Saying that every people has a guide borrowed a word from the working economy of travel rather than from religious vocabulary.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing clause of this ayah, saying that every people has a guide, occurs only here in the Quran. The classical scholars record at least three readings of it, and the grammar does not settle between them. Twenty ayat later the same demand for a sign is quoted again. It is answered there with an entirely different sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage narrows one office and widens another in a single breath. Prophecy is described modestly. It is warning, not the making of proof. Guidance is then extended past the person being addressed, to every community there has ever been. That keeps the message from resting on spectacle. It also refuses to describe any people as simply left alone.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the identical demand later in the same surah and gives it a different answer.
States the same universality from the other side, that every people received a warner.
Answers the same demand by granting the ability and then declining the request.

studies.applyIt: Think of what you are actually responsible for in someone else's life. Usually it is telling them the truth once, clearly, and then being there. The office named here is narrow on purpose. Say the difficult sentence to the person who needs it this week, and then stop, rather than managing the outcome.
studies.explainEasier: People ask why no sign comes down to him from his Lord. The answer is that his job is to warn. And every people has someone to guide them.

studies.title: Everything By Measure
studies.meaning: Knowledge is described at the point where it is least available: what a womb carries, and what it falls short of or gains. Early scholars explain the two verbs as covering shortfall and excess in every sense, in term and number and size. Then a general principle closes the first ayah. Everything with Him has a measure. The second ayah adds four names in quick succession. One pair covers the hidden and the visible. The other pair concerns height.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about it. Pregnancy was the standard example of hidden knowledge in that world, since nothing about its outcome could be settled in advance. The ayah belongs to a passage arguing from the ordered world towards a claim about knowledge. It follows a description of the sun and moon running to fixed terms.

keyTerms.note: The verb for water sinking away or a level dropping, and it occurs only here in the Quran. Using a word from wells and floods of a womb makes a hidden process physical without making it visible.

From the root for capacity and for determining an amount. It names a quantity fixed in advance rather than a limit imposed afterwards, which is why the phrase closes a sentence about what nobody can see.
A name occurring only in this ayah. Its form implies rising above something rather than simply being high, which places it deliberately at the end of a sentence about knowing the hidden and the seen.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing about a pregnancy could be settled in advance. Whether the child lived. Whether the mother lived. Whether it was one or two. How long it would take. All of it was waiting. In a society where a household's future turned on sons and on survival, this was the sharpest example of something wholly outside anyone's knowledge. Everyone had lived through the waiting.
studies.didYouKnow: Both the verb for decrease in the first ayah and the divine name at the end of the second occur only here in the whole Quran. The passage sets a word borrowed from wells and falling water levels beside a name found nowhere else. It does so inside two short ayat about what cannot be seen.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage moves from one specific unknown to a general claim, and then to names. That order matters. It grounds an abstract statement about knowledge in the one uncertainty everybody has actually lived through, and only then makes it general. The phrase about measure does something quiet as well. What is hidden from people is not undecided in itself. It is only unavailable to them.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same item among the things reserved to God's knowledge, in a similar closing formula.
States the same reservation of hidden knowledge and extends it down to a falling leaf.
Uses the same idea of a fixed term, applied there to the sun and to the moon.

studies.applyIt: Pick the thing you are currently waiting on with no way to hurry it: a diagnosis, a decision, a birth. Say to yourself once, plainly, that it already has a measure even though you do not have it. That is not resignation. It is the difference between an unknown quantity and no quantity at all.
studies.explainEasier: God knows what every mother carries, and how much a womb loses or gains. Everything he makes has a set measure. He knows what is hidden and what is seen.

studies.title: Alike, Whispered Or Shouted
studies.meaning: Four conditions are named and then flattened into one. Concealing your speech or announcing it. Hiding by night or moving about by day. The ayah says they are the same. What is being described is not surveillance but the absence of a difference. Early scholars note that the four cases cover the two resources a person actually uses to hide, sound and darkness. The sentence removes both at once, and says nothing about consequences.
studies.historicalContext: The surah carries a Medinan classification, with disagreement recorded by early scholars. The ayah follows straight on from a description of God knowing what a womb carries. It continues the same argument from what cannot be seen. Early scholars report no occasion for it. They read it as belonging to the surah's running case about knowledge rather than to any particular incident.

keyTerms.note: The verb for keeping something inside, from a root that also gives the word for a secret. It covers whispering and thinking without speaking, so the first pair reaches below anything audible.

A participle meaning one who seeks concealment, with the effort built into the form. It names the act of hiding rather than the state of being hidden, which is what makes it comparable to the openness beside it.
A rare word occurring only here, for moving freely along a road. Its root connects with water running loose, so the picture is of somebody flowing along in the open with no thought of being watched.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night was genuine cover in a world with no lamps outside the house. Anyone with something to arrange did it after dark, and a man moving at night was assumed to be hiding something. The two halves of this ayah, sound and darkness, were the only two resources a person had. Removing both left nothing anyone in that world would have called private.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for moving about openly by day occurs only in this ayah in the whole Quran. Its root is connected with water flowing free of any channel. The line pairs it against a word for actively hiding. The two halves describe the extremes of a range, and then declare the entire range equal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The claim is about equivalence rather than about exposure. Nothing here says that hidden things will be revealed to other people. What is denied is that hiding makes any difference to the one being spoken about. That is a gentler statement than it first sounds, and it is also more thorough, since it removes the distinction rather than threatening a disclosure at some later point.

crossReferences.why: Establishes the knowledge of what is hidden that this ayah then applies to human conduct.
Makes the same point about speech and adds a level lying below the secret itself.
Uses the same pairing of concealed and open speech and arrives at the same conclusion.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between how you speak about someone to their face and behind them. Not to feel guilty about it; just measure the gap once, honestly, this week. Then close it by a single degree in one conversation. The ayah says the two versions are already one. You are only catching up with that.
studies.explainEasier: It makes no difference to God whether you whisper or shout. It makes no difference whether you hide in the dark or walk about in daylight. He knows it all the same.

studies.title: Guardians And The Inward Change
studies.meaning: Two claims stand side by side. Angels attend each person, taking over from one another, watching from in front and behind by God's command. Early scholars read the opening word as guardians in shifts, and some link it to the recording angels. Then the sentence turns inward. God does not change a people's state until they change what is inside them. So change starts in the shared self, not in the setting. The closing lines shut off any idea of control.
studies.historicalContext: Early sources argue over where this surah belongs. Some place it in the late Meccan years. Others place it in Medina. The surah itself moves between the two voices. No agreed occasion is reported for this ayah. The chapter's running argument answers demands for a miracle. It points instead to the ordinary order of the world, and to the moral order that runs beside it.

keyTerms.note: A plural from a root meaning to follow on someone's heels. The word carries shift work. One group leaves as the next arrives, so the watch is never left empty, even for a moment.
The word covers the self, the soul and the inner life at once. The ayah puts the state of a people there, not in what surrounds them. That placing is what gives the sentence its force.
The root also gives the words for nearness, friendship and power. It names someone close enough to defend you and strong enough to be worth having. The ayah denies any such figure beside God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In seventh-century Arabia, protection was a named tie between people, not an idea. A traveller crossing tribal country needed a patron who would answer for him. A man without one could be robbed, and nothing would happen to the robber. Clients attached themselves to strong houses for exactly this reason. The closing line of the ayah takes that whole system and says the patron who finally counts is not a man at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens with four separate letters. That set appears nowhere else in the Quran. The surahs on either side, 10, 11, 12, 14 and 15, open with a three-letter set instead. The chapter is named for thunder because of one ayah a little further on, where thunder is described as praising God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah holds two things that people often set against each other. Human choice is real. The state of a community follows from what its members become inside, so history is not simply laid on them. Yet the same sentence denies anyone a hold over God. What He wills for a people cannot be turned aside. Taken together, effort matters without settling the outcome. That is a narrower claim than either fatalism or self-reliance, and an easier one to live with.

crossReferences.why: Says the same rule in reverse: God does not take back a blessing until a people change.
Names the two recording angels seated on either side, another form of the watch described here.
Describes guardians sent over each person until the appointed time arrives.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have been waiting on someone else to fix. Before you think about the situation again, name one thing in yourself that would have to move first: an assumption, a resentment, a habit of putting it off. Write that one thing down. You are not solving it today. You are locating where the sentence says change begins.
studies.explainEasier: God sends angels to watch over every person. They guard from in front and behind. God does not change how things are for a group of people until they change what is inside themselves.

studies.title: The Thunder Praises Him
studies.meaning: Lightning is described by the two responses it produces at once, fear and hope, which in a dry country are one event seen twice. Then heavy clouds are raised up. The second ayah gives the surah its name: thunder glorifies with praise, and the angels do so out of awe of Him. Early scholars divide over whether the thunder's praise is meant literally or names a creature doing what it was made for. The ayah ends by noting that people argue throughout.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about it. This is the ayah the chapter is named after. The classical sources report questions being put about thunder and lightning, and they preserve more than one account of the occasion. They agree on what the passage does. It answers a question about natural events by describing them as acts of praise, not by explaining any mechanism.

keyTerms.note: Two accusatives describing the state of the person watching. The same flash carries both, because a storm in that country meant grazing and full cisterns, and also a valley filling faster than a person can walk.
An adjective of weight applied to clouds. It describes what they are carrying rather than how they look, which is how a farmer rather than a poet picks a cloud out of the sky.
A rare word whose sense early scholars discuss at length, ranging from sheer power to devising and stratagem. They record the range rather than settling it, and the word appears only in this ayah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A storm in Arabia was watched with complete attention. Rain meant grazing and full cisterns for a season, and the same storm could send a wall of water down a dry valley and take a camp with it. People read cloud weight and wind direction the way a sailor reads a sea. The two words for fear and hope here describe standing outside and watching.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for thunder occurs twice in the Quran, at 2:19 and here, and this surah is named after the second of them. So the chapter carries the name of something mentioned once inside it. That is not unusual: several surahs take their names from a detail in a single ayah rather than from their subject.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a question about weather by reassigning it. Thunder is not explained; it is described as an act of praise, and the angels are placed in the same clause doing the same thing out of awe. That puts a natural process and a class of creatures inside one activity. The final clause then sets human argument against the whole scene, and offers no comment on it.

crossReferences.why: Uses thunder and lightning as an extended image, in the only other place thunder is named.
Repeats the same phrase about fear and hope, and continues into rain reviving dead earth.
States as a general principle what this ayah says here about thunder in particular.

studies.applyIt: Next time there is a storm, go and stand where you can watch it for two minutes rather than checking the forecast. Notice that you feel two things at once, and that the ayah names both without asking you to choose. Then notice what the noise is being described as doing.
studies.explainEasier: God shows you the lightning, and it makes you afraid and hopeful at the same time. He raises the heavy rain clouds. The thunder praises him, and so do the angels.

studies.title: Hands Held Out To Water
studies.meaning: A comparison that turns on one physical detail. The call that is true belongs to God, and what else is called upon answers nothing at all. Then the image arrives: a man stretching his open hands out towards water so that it will reach his mouth, and it never does. Early scholars explain the picture as somebody at the edge of a well reaching for water he cannot lift, or as somebody holding out cupped hands and waiting. Either way the failure is built into the posture.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about it. The image assumes a listener who has drawn water from a deep well with rope and bucket. That was the ordinary experience of the entire audience. The passage belongs to the surah's central argument about what can and cannot respond. It follows the description of thunder and lightning under order.

keyTerms.note: The phrase can mean the call that is rightly directed, or the calling of the One who is real. Early scholars record both, and the ambiguity is productive rather than confusing, since either reading fits the image that follows.
From the verb to spread something open, used of a hand laid flat. The participle keeps the man frozen mid-gesture, which is why the comparison reads like a picture rather than a story.
The word for losing a road, so a prayer described this way is not refused but misdirected. The failure lies in where it is aimed rather than in whether the person meant it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wells in Arabia were deep, and drawing from them was work. A rope, a leather bucket, sometimes an animal walking to raise the load. Everyone had stood at the lip of one and looked down at water they could see and could not reach. The gesture in this ayah is hands held out towards water that will not climb. Nobody needed that explained.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison in this ayah is unusual in the Quran for having no movement in it. Most of its images run through a small sequence: rain falling and plants growing, a spider building a house, a flood raising froth. This one holds a single posture, hands extended and water below and nothing happening. The stillness is the point.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the fault in direction rather than in effort. The man in the image is trying, and the trying is described with sympathy. What is wrong is where his hands are pointed. That has a real consequence for how prayer is understood here. Being sincere is not what makes a call work. A genuine appeal to something that cannot answer stays genuine and stays unanswered.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same point about what cannot respond, with a different image for the smallness involved.
States the positive form of the same relation, that a call rightly directed is answered.
Uses another concrete comparison to make the same argument about sheer capacity.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you keep hoping will fix something, and ask honestly whether it can. A promotion, a move, a person changing. The ayah does not say stop wanting it. It says notice where your hands are pointed, and then point some of that effort somewhere that can actually reach back.
studies.explainEasier: Calling on God is the real call. Calling on anything else is like a man holding his hands out to water in a deep well, waiting for it to come up to his mouth. It never does.

studies.title: Even Their Shadows Bow
studies.meaning: One sentence covers everything existing in two realms, and then adds something nobody would have listed. Whoever is in the heavens and the earth prostrates, willingly or unwillingly. So do their shadows, morning and late afternoon. Early scholars explain the unwilling part this way. Every created thing bows to the order it runs under, whatever its owner intends. The shadows are the surprise. A person may refuse, and the shape they cast still moves exactly as the sun requires.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about it. This is one of the places in the Quran where a reader traditionally bows down in prostration. The classical sources record it. Printed copies mark it in the margin. The ayah closes the surah's first long argument from the natural world. After it, the address turns to direct questions.

keyTerms.note: The verb for lowering the face to the ground. Applied to everything in existence it must cover more than the human posture, and early scholars read it as submission expressed in whatever way a given thing is capable of.
Two states named together, which is what makes the claim total. The second word is the one used elsewhere in the Quran for something genuinely hated, so nobody's reluctance is being denied here.
A plural for the stretch between the sun's decline and sunset. Pairing it with early morning names the two times of day when shadows are longest and their movement is easiest to see.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Arabia was told by shadow. The length of a man's shadow set the hours for prayer, for travel and for rest, and children learned to read it long before they learned anything written. Watching a shadow lengthen and swing round was the ordinary way of knowing where you stood in the day. This ayah takes that daily observation and calls it worship.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the places in the Quran where a prostration is traditionally made by the reciter. Printed copies carry a mark in the margin to show it. The ayah describes prostration and then occasions one. A reader who follows the practice performs the very act the sentence is in the middle of describing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes submission a fact about the world before it is a choice made by a person. That does not collapse the difference between willing and unwilling, since both are named in the same breath. What it removes is the option of standing outside the arrangement altogether. Adding the shadows makes it physical: even the part of you that follows no decision of yours is already doing this.

crossReferences.why: Develops the same observation about shadows at greater length and reaches the same conclusion.
Uses the identical pairing of willing and unwilling submission for the same total claim.
Extends prostration to things that cannot choose, in a shorter and starker form.

studies.applyIt: Go out in the late afternoon and look at your own shadow for a moment, and let the ayah's claim sit on it. Whatever you have decided today, that has been moving all afternoon without consulting you. It is a small thing to notice and it puts the rest of the day in a different proportion.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth bows down to God, whether it wants to or not. Even the shadows bow, in the morning and in the late afternoon.

studies.title: Are Darkness And Light Equal
studies.meaning: A cross-examination carried out entirely through one imperative. The opening question is put and then answered in the same breath, since nobody disputed the answer. Three further challenges follow, each introduced the same way. One is about protectors who cannot help even themselves. One asks whether the blind and the seeing are equal. One asks whether anyone else has created something that could be confused with His creation. The last line closes the case rather than arguing on.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about it. Its audience already accepted a creator while giving their worship elsewhere. That is exactly the gap this ayah works in. Early scholars note the structure: a question answered by the questioner. They read it as setting common ground first, before the harder questions are put.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning nearness. The word names those you turn to for help and who owe you help in return, so denying the capacity denies the relationship rather than the existence of the objects.

A plural, where light in the same clause stays singular, and the Quran keeps that asymmetry throughout. Darkness comes in kinds and layers; light does not, and the grammar says so before any argument does.
An intensive form from a root meaning to overpower. Paired with the One, it says that singleness here is not merely a count but a relation in which nothing else can hold its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A patron was a practical arrangement rather than a feeling. You attached yourself to someone stronger. In return they answered for you in a dispute and stood beside you in a fight. Asking whether these patrons could help or harm even themselves was a question in the language of contracts. It asked what, exactly, the arrangement delivered.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah contains the imperative Say five times. That is more than any other ayah in the Quran, and the next highest has four. Four of the five introduce a question, and one introduces its answer. So the whole line is built as an instructed cross-examination rather than as a statement of belief.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument works by asking rather than by asserting, and every question has an answer the listener already holds. That is a particular strategy. Nothing new is introduced, only the consequences of what had already been granted. The pairing at the end is the sharpest part. It says that being one is not a matter of counting, but of there being nothing else able to stand against it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same pair of comparisons and extends the list to shade, heat and the dead.
Puts the same challenge again later in the surah, asking them to name what they have set up.
Uses the same technique of a question answered by the questioner, in the ayah with the next most imperatives.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you rely on more than you would admit and ask the ayah's second question about it: can it help or harm even itself? A reputation, a savings account, a person's approval. You are not being asked to give it up. You are being asked to be accurate about what it can carry.
studies.explainEasier: Ask them who made the sky and the earth. Say it is God. Then ask if darkness and light are the same, or if a blind man and a seeing man are the same. They are not.

studies.title: Froth And What Remains
studies.meaning: A double image, both drawn from things that separate under pressure. Rain falls and each valley carries what it can hold, so the flood raises a scum on the surface; metal heated for jewellery or tools throws up the same worthless layer. Early scholars read the water as revelation and the differing riverbeds as hearts of differing capacity. The froth is swept off. What actually serves people stays in the ground.
studies.historicalContext: The chapter argues throughout with people who demand a spectacular sign. Early sources divide over whether it is late Meccan or Medinan. No particular occasion is reported for this ayah. The parable answers a live question of that time. The question was how to tell a true message from an impressive one, when both arrived with confidence and both drew followers.

keyTerms.note: The word for the foam on a flood and the dross that rises off molten metal. It is not nothing; it is the most visible thing in the vessel, which is exactly the point of the comparison.
From the root for measuring and apportioning. Each channel takes the volume its own size allows, so the same rainfall produces very different streams without any difference in what was sent down.

A verb of staying put rather than merely surviving. It suggests settling and taking up residence, which is why the translation reaches for the ground: the useful thing sinks in and stays where it is needed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both halves of the parable were ordinary sights. Arabian valleys ran dry for most of the year, then filled violently after rain. Anyone who had stood at a wadi in flood had watched a brown line of foam. Torn brush rode along the top of it. Smiths working silver for bracelets or bronze for pots skimmed the same rising scum off the melt and threw it away.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah runs two separate parables into one sentence and closes by naming what it has just done, saying twice that God sets forth comparisons. That doubling is rare. The classical commentators treat the pair as deliberate: one image from water and one from fire, so that no listener could claim the point depended on a single kind of example.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truth is measured here by what it leaves behind, not by how it looks on arrival. The parable grants falsehood real prominence in the moment. It rides visibly on top, and the image does not pretend otherwise. What tells the two apart is how long they last and what good they do. The claim about God is indirect but firm. He sets the terms of the sorting. The sorting happens in time, not by argument.

crossReferences.why: States the same outcome without the image: falsehood is by nature something that vanishes.
Uses water again for the world's brief flourishing, the other half of the same lesson.
Sets a good word and a bad word against each other as a rooted tree and an uprooted one.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you took seriously a year ago that has since evaporated: an argument online, a piece of news, a plan that felt urgent. Notice how much attention it took at the time. Then look at what you have kept doing quietly all year without anyone noticing. Give one of those quiet things ten extra minutes today.
studies.explainEasier: When rain fills a valley, foam floats on top and then gets swept away. The water that soaks into the ground is what helps people. Truth is like the water. What is false is like the foam.

studies.title: Everything On Earth, Twice Over
studies.meaning: Two outcomes are set against each other, and the second is described at far greater length. Those who answer their Lord get the best. Those who do not are given an imagined case before they are given anything else. If they owned everything on earth and as much again, they would offer it to ransom themselves. Early scholars note that the sentence never says the offer would be refused. It simply describes what they would do, which is worse.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among early scholars. This ayah closes the section that began with the parable of the flood and the froth, turning from images to consequences. The construction it uses, everything on earth and as much again, appears in two other places in the Quran. In all three it describes a ransom that cannot work.

keyTerms.note: The verb for answering a call by acting, not merely by replying to it. The whole division in this ayah rests on it, so what separates the two groups is a response rather than an opinion held.
From the verb to pay a redemption price, used of buying back a captive. It names an ordinary transaction of that world, which is what makes the hypothetical concrete rather than merely rhetorical.

A word for something spread out to lie on, used elsewhere in the Quran of the earth prepared for people. Applying it here makes the destination a bed, and that is where the bitterness of the phrase sits.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ransom was a working institution. Captives were bought back. Blood money was counted out in camels. A man in trouble worked out exactly what his family could raise, and everyone knew the going rates. Describing someone who would hand over the whole earth twice over named a debt outside every scale people had. It used a vocabulary they used constantly.
studies.didYouKnow: The construction used here, everything on earth and as much again beside it, occurs three times in the Quran, at 5:36, in this ayah, and at 39:47. In all three it describes a ransom that would be offered and does not work. The Quran reuses one hypothetical amount whenever it wants to name a price nobody could meet.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah measures a loss by what somebody would pay to avoid it, which is a human way of stating a size. It also makes the division turn on responding rather than on knowing. The line falls between those who acted on a call and those who did not. And the closing word chooses a household image, a bed, which makes the description permanent rather than merely frightening.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical hypothetical about everything on earth and as much again, offered as a ransom.
Applies the same measure to the earth full of gold, and says it would not be accepted.
Describes the people on the other side of this division, and what they actually did.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you would pay to get out of something you have committed to and are dreading. Put a number on it, honestly. Then notice that you could simply do the thing instead, and that the doing is almost always cheaper. This ayah measures a loss by its ransom price for exactly that reason.
studies.explainEasier: Those who answer their Lord get the best. Those who turn away would give away everything on earth, twice over, to buy their way out. Their place is a hard one to rest in.

studies.title: The Knower And The Blind
studies.meaning: A question with no answer supplied, because none is needed. It asks whether the one who knows that what was sent down is the truth is like one who is blind. The comparison sets knowledge against a physical incapacity, which puts the difference outside the range of opinion. Then a restriction follows. Only those with kernels remember. Early scholars note that the word names an inner core rather than intelligence. What is required is not cleverness but something underneath it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about it. This ayah opens a long passage listing the qualities of the people it names. That list runs through the next several ayat and is answered by an opposite list afterwards. The comparison with blindness picks up a pairing used a few ayat earlier, where blind and seeing were set against darkness and light.

keyTerms.note: An interrogative that expects the listener to complete the sentence themselves. Arabic often leaves the second half of such comparisons unstated, and the omission is exactly what gives the line its force.
The plain word for loss of sight. Using a physical condition for a failure of recognition removes the question from the realm of preference, since nobody argues about whether they can see.
The plural of the word for the inner part of a nut or seed, the part that is eaten. People described this way are named for having a core, and the phrase occurs seven times in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blindness was common and untreated. Sand, sun and infection took the sight of a great many people. Every settlement had someone who moved by touch and by memory. The comparison would not have landed as an insult so much as a fact of the neighbourhood. It described a real limit nobody chose and nobody could argue their way out of.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for those with kernels occurs seven times in the Quran. It is built on the word for the edible core of a nut, not on any word for the mind. Arabic separates what a shell holds from the shell itself. So the people it names are described by what is inside them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah compares two conditions rather than two positions, and that changes what kind of disagreement is being described. One person has access and the other does not. Neither is shown as having argued their way there. That makes the passage less about persuasion than about capacity. The closing restriction says plainly that remembering is something only certain people do.

crossReferences.why: Sets up the same comparison between blind and seeing, a few ayat before this one.
States the same comparison as a flat denial rather than as an open question.
Puts the identical question about knowledge and closes with the same phrase about kernels.

studies.applyIt: Think about something you learned once and have not thought about since. Knowledge here is not information held but something a person is currently seeing by. Pick one thing you know and act on it today in a way you have not done for a while. That is the difference the ayah is drawing.
studies.explainEasier: The ayah asks if a person who knows the truth is the same as a person who is blind to it. They are not the same. Only people who think deeply take it in.

studies.title: What Is Meant To Be Joined
studies.meaning: Two ayat from a longer list, and each item is a habit rather than an achievement. Fulfilling the agreement with God, and not unravelling the pledge. Then joining what God has commanded to be joined. Early scholars read that chiefly as ties of kinship, and more widely as everything a person is meant to keep connected. The last two items are inward and use different verbs: an awe that keeps someone careful, and a fear of one particular outcome.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded. The list running through these ayat is answered by an exact inversion a few lines later. There the same three items appear as breaking, cutting and spreading corruption. Early scholars treat the two passages as a matched pair. They note that the phrase about joining appears only here, in its negative form there, and once in surah 2.

keyTerms.gloss: they fulfil, they pay in full
keyTerms.note: The verb for discharging an obligation completely, used of settling a debt or measuring out goods without shortfall. It names completion rather than intention, which is why the whole list is made of things done.
From a root meaning to tie firmly, the strongest word for an agreement in the Quran. The verb paired with it means to unpick something twisted, so the image behind the line is a rope and its fibres.
A verb for fear mixed with reverence, distinct from the plain word for fright used in the very next clause. The Quran usually attaches it to those who know what they are dealing with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Kinship in Arabia was not a feeling. It was infrastructure. Your relatives fed you in famine. They paid your blood money, married your daughters and buried you. Cutting the tie meant stepping out of the only welfare system there was. When these ayat name joining what God commanded to be joined, the first listeners heard something with real costs attached.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about joining what God has commanded to be joined occurs three times in the Quran. It is here in the positive, four ayat later in the negative, and once at 2:27, also negative. So this is the only place in the whole book where it appears as something people actually do. Everywhere else it names something they fail to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The list is built out of upkeep rather than achievement. Keeping an agreement. Not cutting a connection. Holding a particular kind of fear. None of these produces anything visible, and all of them are undone by neglect rather than by a decision. That says something about how the passage understands a life of faith. It is why the inverted list a few ayat later reads as things allowed to fall apart.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same list with three further items and names what those described will receive.
Gives the exact inversion of these two ayat, with the same items turned into breaking and cutting.
Uses the same phrase about severing what God commanded to be joined, in its negative form.

studies.applyIt: Name one connection you have not cut but have stopped maintaining: an old friend, an aunt, a neighbour. Nothing happened; it just thinned. The verb in this ayah is joining, which is ongoing work rather than a decision. Do one small piece of that work this week without explaining the gap.
studies.explainEasier: These are people who keep their word to God and do not break their promise. They keep their family ties joined. They hold God in awe, and they are afraid of a bad end.

studies.title: Repelling Bad With Good
studies.meaning: The list continues with four more items, and the last is the most unusual. Patience is qualified by a purpose, seeking the face of their Lord, which separates it from simple endurance. Prayer is kept up. Giving is done both secretly and openly, so neither hiding nor showing is made the correct mode. Then the final item. They push the bad thing away with a good one, which describes a response to hostility rather than an avoidance of it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded by early scholars. The list these ayat form is one of the Quran's several descriptions of the people it praises. Early scholars note that this one is unusually balanced between inward states and outward acts. The final item, meeting bad with good, is repeated elsewhere in the Quran at greater length.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for doing something for a person's sake alone. Naming the face rather than a reward makes the aim the relation itself, which is what separates this patience from simply outlasting a difficulty.
Two states named together rather than one preferred. The Quran elsewhere praises hidden giving, so the pairing here declines to make secrecy a rule and leaves the manner to the situation.
The verb for shoving something off, occurring twice in the Quran. It is physical, so what is described is not tolerance of a wrong but an active countermove made with that wrong's opposite.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Answering an insult was all but required in Arabia. A slight left unanswered lowered a family, and poets were engaged to reply in kind. The expected response to a bad thing was a matching bad thing, publicly and promptly. Meeting it with a good one would have looked to the first listeners less like restraint than like a move nobody had thought of.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for pushing something away occurs only twice in the Quran. Its other appearance is at 28:54, in a passage describing people who repel bad with good. They are said to receive their reward twice over. Both places attach the same doubled reward to the same unusual response.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The list joins inward and outward without ranking them, and its last item is the demanding one. Repelling a bad thing with a good one is not forgiveness, which absorbs, and it is not retaliation, which matches. It is a third move, and it requires a person to have something ready to give at the exact moment they have been given nothing. That is why patience is named first.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for repelling bad with good, and attaches a doubled reward to it.
Elaborates the same instruction, and describes what it can do to a hostile relationship.
Gives the earlier items of the same list, which this ayah completes before naming the reward.

studies.applyIt: Pick the person who has been small with you recently and do one specific good thing for them this week that they will notice. Not a grand gesture and not a lecture. The ayah names a push, so it should cost you something and it should land. Then let the matter drop entirely.
studies.explainEasier: They are patient because they want their Lord's pleasure. They pray. They give in secret and in the open. When someone treats them badly, they answer with something good instead.

studies.title: Reunion Behind Every Gate
studies.meaning: The reward promised in the ayat before is now named, and its first feature is company. People enter the gardens together with whoever among their parents, spouses and children was fit to enter. Early scholars note that this joining is a gift. Being related to the righteous does not by itself qualify anyone. Angels come in from every gate with one greeting. The reason they give is endurance, not achievement.
studies.historicalContext: Some early authorities place the surah in the late Meccan years. Others place it in Medina. These two ayat close a list that begins several verses earlier. It names people who keep their agreements, join what God commanded to be joined, pray, give openly and in secret, and answer harm with good. No particular occasion is reported. The phrase about joining what should be joined was widely taken to include family ties. That makes a promise of reunion the natural answer to it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to stay in a place permanently, the same root behind the word for a mine, which is where a metal sits fixed. It names permanence rather than pleasure.
The verb covers restraint under pressure, not calm feeling. The greeting attributes entry to this, which places a lifetime of holding on above any single act as the thing being honoured.

A noun of consequence, from the root for what follows behind. It frames the home not as a place but as the end a life arrives at, so the praise is for where the road came out rather than for the scenery.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A house in that world was a compound. A family's standing showed in who lived inside its walls. Death broke these households up again and again. Children were buried before parents. Wives were lost in childbirth. Sons were killed in raids. The move to Medina scattered more of them, cutting believers off from relatives who stayed behind. A promise that the household would be gathered again, entered through more than one gate at once, answered a real loss.
studies.didYouKnow: The angels' greeting arrives with no verb of speaking in front of it. Arabic lets that word be understood rather than written, and the early grammarians say so here. The greeting reaches the reader as suddenly as it reaches the people at the gate. The same words are spoken at the gates in surah 39. There the reason given is goodness, not endurance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are set out at once. The gardens are described in terms of company, so being saved is not pictured as a lonely state. Family ties are carried across into it as a gift, not as something inherited. The reason given for the welcome is endurance under hardship. That turns an ordinary life of holding on into the substance of the achievement, rather than the waiting before it.

crossReferences.why: Describes descendants joined to their parents without any reduction in what the parents earned.
Gives the same arrival scene, gates opened and keepers greeting those who come.
A prayer of the angels asking that the righteous among parents, spouses and offspring be admitted too.

studies.applyIt: Name the person in your family you would most want to find waiting on the other side. Then send them something today: a message, a call, five minutes of your attention. The ayah ties the reunion to endurance. Holding on with your own relatives in this life is usually the plain, everyday form of that.
studies.explainEasier: Good people will go into the gardens. The good members of their families will be there too. Angels will come in through every gate. They will say peace to them, because they kept going through hard times.

studies.title: The Same List, Reversed
studies.meaning: An inversion exact enough to work as a mirror. The positive items of the earlier passage return as their opposites, in the same order. The agreement broken after it was pledged. The connection severed rather than joined. Corruption spread in the land. Only the third is new in kind. Early scholars read the added item as a consequence rather than as a further offence. What is described is what a dismantled structure produces on its own.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with early scholars recording disagreement. This ayah closes the second half of a matched pair. The first half runs from 13:20 to 13:22. Describing a group and then inverting the description item by item is a technique used elsewhere in the Quran. Early scholars point to this pair as one of the tidiest examples of it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for undoing something twisted back into its separate fibres, the exact opposite of the word for a binding pledge that follows it. Both words come from the world of rope-making.

The plain verb for cutting, set against the verb for joining used in the earlier passage. Arabic uses this pair constantly of kinship, so severing and joining are the standard terms for how relatives behave.
From a root meaning to expel and drive away. It names distance rather than pain, which fits a passage about cutting connections: the consequence has the same shape as the offence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was the heaviest sanction an Arabian tribe could apply. A man cut off from his people kept his life and lost everything that protected it. He could be killed on the road, with nobody obliged to answer for him. Naming the consequence with a word that means being driven away spoke to the most feared condition in that society.
studies.didYouKnow: The first three clauses of this ayah appear almost word for word at 2:27, near the start of the Quran's second surah. Here they also form the exact reverse of the list at 13:20 and 13:21, using the opposite of each verb. So one sentence does one job in the earlier surah and a second, structural job in this one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the two lists inside one surah, in the same order, makes a point neither could make alone. The same three things are at stake for everybody. What separates the two groups is direction rather than subject matter. It also implies that corruption in the land is not a separate kind of wrong. It is what follows once pledges and connections stop being kept up.

crossReferences.why: Gives the positive list this ayah reverses, item by item and in the same order.
Carries the same three clauses in almost identical words, of those who break God's covenant.
Joins severing ties of kinship to corruption in the land, and names what results from it.

studies.applyIt: Look at the three items in order: a promise, a connection, and the state of the place around you. They are listed in that sequence for a reason. Check the first one this week. Is there a commitment you made and have quietly stopped honouring? Restart it before looking at anything further down the list.
studies.explainEasier: Others break the promise they made to God. They cut the ties they were told to keep. They spread trouble in the land. The curse is on them, and a bad home waits for them.

studies.title: Spread Out And Measured
studies.meaning: A single pair of verbs covers the whole distribution of provision. He spreads it wide for whom He wills, and He narrows it. Neither is explained and neither is called a reward. Then the sentence turns to a reaction, that they rejoice in the life of this world. The closing clause supplies a measurement rather than a rebuke. Set against what follows, this life is only a passing enjoyment. The word for it is the one used of a traveller's baggage.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded. The ayah follows a passage about those who keep their pledges and those who break them. It then interrupts that sorting with a statement about wealth which does not track it at all. Early scholars read the placement as deliberate. Provision is described right after a passage about deserving, and it is not attached to it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for laying something open and flat, used of a hand opened or a cloth spread. Provision is pictured as an area rather than a quantity, which is why its opposite here is narrowing rather than subtracting.
From the root for measuring and for capacity. It means making something exact and therefore tight, so the two verbs together describe a width being set rather than a gift given or withheld.
The same word names the baggage a traveller carries and the pleasure a thing gives. Both senses assume a journey, so what is described is equipment for the road rather than the destination itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in that world plainly failed to follow character. A dishonest merchant prospered. An honest one lost a caravan to raiders. Everybody could name examples of both. Arabian moral thinking often reached for luck or for family line to explain it. This ayah declines both explanations. It gives the distribution to God and leaves the reason unstated.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about provision being spread wide and narrowed occurs nine times in the Quran, across nine different surahs. That makes it one of the most repeated formulas in the whole book. The subject beside it changes every time. Only the sentence itself stays fixed, which is what gives it the feel of a standing rule.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah separates provision from merit, and then measures the whole of this life against what follows it. That is two moves in one line, and the second protects the first. If wealth is not a verdict, then its presence or its absence could produce a false conclusion. Naming this life as passing takes the ground out from under both conclusions at once.

crossReferences.why: Gives one reason the narrowing half of this ayah should not be read as a punishment.
Names the two false conclusions people draw from wealth given and from wealth withheld.
Returns later in the surah to the comparison between this life's condition and the next.

studies.applyIt: Notice the last time you read someone's comfort or difficulty as a statement about them, including your own. Write the sentence you actually thought, then set it beside this ayah. It attributes the distribution and refuses to explain it. Try leaving one such situation unexplained for a week and see what that costs you.
studies.explainEasier: God gives lots of money to some people and little to others. It is not a prize. Some are very happy with this life, but this life is small next to the one that comes after.

studies.title: Whoever Turns Back Is Guided
studies.meaning: The same demand quoted twenty ayat earlier is quoted again, and this time the answer is different. There the reply defined a messenger's office; here it describes how guidance actually moves. God lets go astray whom He wills, and guides to Himself whoever turns back. Early scholars note the asymmetry in the sentence, since the second half names a condition and the first does not. The way in is described and the way out is left unexplained.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about it. The repetition of the demand is deliberate, and early scholars discuss why two answers are given. The ayah belongs to the surah's closing section. That section returns to questions raised at the opening and handles them more briefly the second time, since the argument has already been set out at length.

keyTerms.note: The causative of the verb for losing a road. Early scholars are careful with it, reading it as leaving somebody to a direction already chosen rather than as pushing them onto that road.
A small phrase doing real work in the sentence. Guidance here is given a destination, so being guided is described as arriving somewhere rather than as receiving information about a route.
The verb for coming back to a place you had left, and used of returning repeatedly. It names a movement rather than a state, so what qualifies a person is a turn they have already made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In desert travel, going astray and being guided were not figures of speech. A party half a day off the track could die. The difference between arriving and not arriving often came down to whether somebody turned back at the right moment rather than pressing on. Turning back was the skill that saved people, and everyone who travelled knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: The demand quoted at the start of this ayah is repeated word for word from 13:7, twenty ayat earlier, and answered completely differently the second time. The first answer describes what a messenger is; this one describes how guidance moves. The Quran quotes one objection twice inside a single surah and declines to give it the same reply.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah sets two clauses side by side that are not symmetrical, and the asymmetry is the point. Being left to stray is stated without a condition; being guided is given one, and that condition is a turn the person makes. The door is therefore described only from the inside. It also names the destination of guidance as God rather than as being correct about something.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the identical demand earlier in the surah and answers it with a different sentence.
Uses the same phrase about guiding to Himself whoever turns back towards Him.
Describes the same turn in more detail, and names what it opens for a person.

studies.applyIt: There is a direction you know you have been going in for a while, and a point where you could turn round without anyone noticing. The verb here is simply turning back. Do the smallest version of it today, in private, without announcing anything or working out the whole route first.
studies.explainEasier: People ask again why no sign is sent down to him. The answer is that God lets some people wander off, and he guides to himself anyone who turns back to him.

studies.title: Where Hearts Settle
studies.meaning: The sentence is said, then said again with the order flipped. That turns a description of believers into a general law about hearts. Early scholars read the remembrance both ways: the servant remembering God, and the Quran itself, which is called a reminder. What is promised is not excitement but settling, the state of a thing that has stopped moving. Note that the ayah does not say hearts find answers.
