studies.historicalContext: The ayah comes as the answer to an objection quoted two verses earlier, where opponents ask why no miracle has been sent down. The reply first says that guidance is God's to give and then describes who receives it. The classical sources give no specific occasion. The surah as a whole belongs to the argument with Meccan leaders over what would count as proof, though authorities differ on whether it was revealed there or in Medina.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of ground that is level and of a person who dismounts and stays. It describes a heart that stops casting about, not one that is happy, which is a lower and steadier promise.
The same noun covers calling something to mind, saying it aloud, and the revealed text itself. The ambiguity is not a flaw; the commentators take the ayah in more than one of these senses at once.
From a root meaning to turn over or overturn. The organ is named for its instability, which is why a word for settling is the thing being promised to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel in Arabia meant long stretches with nothing to fix on: sand, stars, the same horizon for days. Caravans navigated by remembered landmarks and by repeated verse, and reciting aloud was how a group kept its bearings and its nerve through a night march. A traveller's worst state was not danger but not knowing where he was. What this ayah offers is steadiness detached from any landmark at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause is built as a mirror. First, believers whose hearts settle by the remembrance of God. Then the remembrance of God, by which hearts settle. Arabic can flip the order because the grammar marks the roles. The flip lifts the statement out of one group and into a rule. The second half is what made this half-ayah quotable on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The claim is about how people are built, not only about God. Hearts are said to have one object that quiets them. So restlessness is a sign of something, not an accident. That leaves room for a believer who is still anxious. The ayah says what settles a heart. It does not offer a method that removes hardship. The promise also comes with no condition about circumstances, so it holds through poverty, illness and grief.

crossReferences.why: Describes hearts that tremble at God's mention, the other movement remembrance produces.
The direct exchange: remember Me and I will remember you.
States the opposite case, a constricted life for whoever turns away from the reminder.

studies.applyIt: Choose a moment you already repeat every day without thinking: the walk from the car, the kettle boiling, the lift. Attach one short phrase of remembrance to it, the same phrase each time. Do not add a new slot to your day. Take a slot that is already empty and put something in it, then leave it alone for a week.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe feel calm inside when they remember God. The verse then says it again, as a rule for everyone. It is remembering God that makes hearts settle down.

studies.title: A Word For Their Happiness
studies.meaning: A short ayah with one strange word inside it. Those who believe and do sound works are given something the Arabic names with a term found nowhere else in the Quran. Early scholars offer several readings: a state of good, gladness, a good outcome, or a named tree in the Garden. They set the range down without choosing. Then a second phrase arrives, a beautiful place of return. That one is ordinary, and it settles the sentence by giving it somewhere to arrive.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded. The ayah comes shortly after the description of hearts settling by remembrance, and it names what those described receive. Early scholars note that the promise here is unusually compressed beside the surah's earlier description of the Gardens. They read the two as filling each other out rather than as alternatives.

keyTerms.note: A form from the root for what is good and pleasant, occurring only here in the Quran. Early scholars offer several readings, including a state of gladness, a good end, and a named tree, and they preserve them all.
A noun of place from the verb to come back. It names a destination defined by returning rather than by arriving, so what is promised is somewhere you go back to rather than somewhere new.
From a root meaning to be in good repair, the same one behind the verb for reconciling people. Good deeds are named as things that work properly rather than as things that earn credit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The word for a place of return had a physical meaning for people who moved with the seasons. A tribe left its grazing ground and came back to it, and the coming back was the point of the leaving. Naming a destination that way told listeners that what was promised was not a strange place. It was the one they had come from, which is a particular kind of comfort.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for what the believers receive occurs only once in the whole Quran. The classical scholars list several readings of it. Among them are a state of gladness, a good end, and a tree in the Garden so large that a rider could travel a long time in its shade. They record those readings side by side without ranking them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah promises something without fully specifying it, and the scholars' inability to settle the word is part of how it works on a reader. What is named clearly is the second half, a place of return. What is left open is the first. That combination gives a definite destination and an indefinite good. It is roughly how the Quran describes what is coming throughout.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same destination at greater length, with who is met there and what is said.
Names the condition of the people this ayah promises, hearts settled by remembrance.
Uses the same word for a place of return, contrasting it with what people are drawn to here.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you look forward to is described to you in detail, and how little of it satisfies when it arrives. This ayah promises something and then refuses to specify it. Try, once this week, wanting something you cannot picture. It is a different exercise from planning, and considerably harder.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe and do good works get something wonderful. The word for it is used only once in the whole Quran. They also get a beautiful place to come home to.

studies.title: He Is My Lord
studies.meaning: The messenger is placed in a line of others and given a task described by one verb: to recite what has been revealed. Then a fact about the audience, that they deny the Merciful, and then a reply made of four short statements. Each one is personal. He is my Lord; there is no god but He; upon Him I rely; and to Him is my turning back. The reply argues nothing at all. It states a position and stops there.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among early scholars. The classical sources report something about the name used here for God, the Merciful. Some people objected to it as an odd way of addressing Him. Several scholars tie this ayah to that objection. The passage belongs to the surah's closing section, where the messenger states his own position rather than defending it.

keyTerms.note: From a root connected both with a mother and with intending a direction. It names a group by what it moves towards rather than by descent, which is why the word can cover a nation and a period at once.
An intensive form built on the root for the womb. The classical sources report that some found this an unfamiliar name to use of God, which is precisely what the ayah is answering here.
A noun from the verb behind repentance, with the possessive attached. It closes the sentence with the speaker's own destination rather than with any claim about the people who have just denied him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names for God varied across Arabia, and different regions used different ones. A name that was ordinary in one place could sound foreign in another. Objecting to a name was a known way of rejecting the thing named without having to argue about it. That is the situation this ayah reports. The reply simply uses the name again.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran records this objection to the name directly at 25:60. There people are told to prostrate to the Merciful, and they answer by asking what the Merciful is. Here the objection is only noted in passing. The response is not an explanation of the name. It is a four-part statement about who the speaker takes his Lord to be.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply is entirely in the first person and makes no claim at all about the objectors. Faced with a rejection of a name, the answer is a statement of one's own position, four clauses long, with no argument and no reproach. That models a kind of response the surah has not yet shown. It puts reliance and return at the end, so the last word concerns where the speaker is going.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same objection to the name directly, put in the form of a question.
Answers the same objection about which name to use, and settles it a different way.
Ends another messenger's reply with the same two statements, reliance and turning back.

studies.applyIt: The next time somebody dismisses something you hold, try answering only about yourself. Not a defence and not a counter-argument. One or two sentences saying what you actually rely on. It is a much shorter reply than the one you were preparing. It ends the exchange without requiring anybody to lose.
studies.explainEasier: The Prophet is told to read out what God sent him, even though those people reject the Merciful. He answers simply. He is my Lord. There is no god but him. I trust him and I turn back to him.

studies.title: Even If Mountains Moved
studies.meaning: A conditional sentence deliberately left unfinished. If there were a recitation that moved mountains, split the earth open, or made the dead speak. Then the second half never arrives. Early scholars discuss the gap at length and supply it as this would be that recitation. The argument then turns. The whole matter belongs to God, and had He willed, everyone would have been guided. So the missing conclusion is answered by a fact about how belief actually works.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with early scholars recording disagreement. The ayah answers the demand for a sign that this surah has already quoted twice. The three examples given are moving mountains, splitting the earth, and speaking to the dead. They are extreme cases. Early scholars read them as the largest signs anyone could ask for, named here in order to be set aside.

keyTerms.note: The passive of the verb for making something travel. The Quran uses it elsewhere of mountains on the last day, so the example named here is not fanciful but taken from what has already been promised.
From the verb to knock or strike hard, so the word names a calamity by its sound. It also titles surah 101, where it becomes a name for the last day itself rather than for any ordinary trouble.
A meeting with a place and a time agreed between two parties. The word occurs four times in the Quran, and the sentence it closes here also closes a prayer near the end of surah 3.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were the fixed points of the landscape. Routes, boundaries and stories were all keyed to them, and they were the standard image for what does not move. Naming the moving of mountains as an imagined sign reached for the least likely event a listener could picture. The ayah names it in order to say that even that would settle nothing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for a striking disaster becomes the title of surah 101, where it names the last day. It occurs five times in the Quran and three of those are packed into the opening three ayat of that very short surah. Here alone it is used of an ordinary calamity rather than of the end of everything.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says that the largest sign anyone could imagine would not produce belief. It gives a reason. Guiding everybody was always available and was not done. That places belief outside the class of things evidence compels, without saying that evidence is worthless. The ayah then closes on a kept appointment, so the argument ends with a promise rather than with a verdict on anyone.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same claim about signs that are demanded, and lists what would still not suffice.
Quotes the demand for a sign that this ayah finally answers at the surah's close.
Closes a prayer with the same sentence about God keeping the appointment He has made.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what would actually change your mind about something you already half doubt. Write the answer down. Then ask whether, if it happened, you would in fact change. Most people discover the honest answer is no, which is what this ayah says about signs, without any reproach attached.
studies.explainEasier: Even if a reading could move mountains, split the earth, or make the dead speak, it would not change them. Everything is up to God. If he had wanted, he could have guided all people.

studies.title: Mocked Before You Too
studies.meaning: A consolation delivered as a piece of history, and the sequence inside it carries the weight. Messengers before were mocked. Those who denied were given a stretch of time. Then they were seized. The final clause is a question with no answer supplied, asking how the consequence turned out to be. Early scholars note that the word used here for granting time appears elsewhere in the Quran too. It always describes an interval that gets mistaken for safety.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among early scholars. This comfort belongs to the closing section. That section returns to the position of the messenger himself, after a long stretch of argument. Early scholars report no particular occasion. They read the pattern named here as the one the surah pointed to earlier, when it spoke of examples that had already passed.

keyTerms.note: A passive form of a verb meaning to make light of something. Mockery is a distinct kind of opposition, since it does not engage a claim but lowers the person carrying it, and the Quran names it separately from denial.
The verb for letting out slack, spoken here in the first person, which is unusual. It occurs in this exact form only twice in the Quran, and both times what follows the interval is a seizure.
From the root for a heel, so what follows wrongdoing is named as the thing coming along behind it. The possessive ending is elided in the Arabic, which gives the closing question its abruptness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon, and there were professionals who dealt in it. Mocking verse was paid for, learned by heart and repeated at gatherings. A well-made line could follow a man for the rest of his life. It could be recited about his children afterwards. Being laughed at there was not a mild social problem. It was a campaign, with a known method and known people to run it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for granting time occurs in this exact first-person past form only twice in the Quran. It is here and at 22:44. In both places what follows immediately is a seizure. The shift into a single speaker for a sentence about respite and consequence is unusual enough that early scholars pause on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The consolation offered here promises neither relief nor vindication. It describes a pattern that has already run, and it ends on a question rather than a claim. That leaves a reader to supply what they already know. It is a particular kind of comfort. Not that this will pass, but that its shape is familiar, and that the interval now being taken for safety has been misread before.

crossReferences.why: Names the same pattern earlier in the surah, of examples that had already passed by.
Explains the same interval from the other side, as a lengthening rather than a favour.
States the same consolation and adds what happened to the mockery itself afterwards.

studies.applyIt: If you are being made a joke of somewhere, resist the two obvious moves: answering in kind, and pretending you have not noticed. Do neither for a week. The ayah offers no strategy and no promise about the mockers, only the observation that this has a known shape. Sometimes that alone is enough to stand in.
studies.explainEasier: Messengers before this one were laughed at too. God gave the people who refused them extra time. Then he took hold of them. The ayah asks how bad that ending turned out to be.

studies.title: Name Them, Then
studies.meaning: Another unfinished comparison. The One standing over every soul with whatever it has earned, and then the sentence breaks off without completing the contrast. What follows is a challenge in two words: name them. Early scholars explain the demand as asking for a description, since anything that could actually be named would need qualities that could be checked. Two alternatives are offered and both are unflattering. One is informing Him of something on earth He does not know. The other is a surface of words.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded. The ayah returns to the challenge put at 13:16 and sharpens it. Early scholars note the unfinished construction and read it as the same technique used earlier in the surah, where a comparison is set up and the listener left to complete it. The closing clause connects the refusal to a scheme made attractive to those making it.

keyTerms.note: The participle of the verb to stand, used of somebody overseeing work or holding a post. It describes an attentive presence rather than knowledge alone, and the phrase it forms here occurs only in this ayah.
Two syllables carrying the whole challenge. Naming in Arabic means giving a description that actually fits, so the demand is for an account that could be examined rather than merely for a label.
The first word means outward or apparent, so the phrase describes words with nothing but an exterior. It names talk that has a shape and no content behind it, which is the second alternative offered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Naming in Arabia was a serious business. A name recorded a quality, an incident or a lineage, and it could be given, earned or lost. Nicknames stuck for generations and were used as arguments in disputes. Demanding that somebody name a thing was asking them to say what it actually was, in front of people who would test the description.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing God as standing over every soul with what it has earned occurs only in this ayah. So does the two-word challenge to name them. The sentence is also incomplete in its grammar. The comparison it opens is never finished, and early scholars supply the missing half from the sense of the surrounding passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The challenge is about knowledge rather than about scoring points. It does not argue that the alternatives are weak. It asks for a description, and then points out that there are only two possibilities if one is supplied. Both of them undo the claim. That shows a position to have no content rather than to be mistaken, which is a different kind of answer and a harder one to meet.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same challenge earlier in the surah, about protectors that cannot help themselves.
Answers the same challenge directly, saying that only the names themselves exist.
Uses the identical question about informing God of something, in almost the same words.

studies.applyIt: Take something you say you believe and try to state it in one sentence that could be checked. Not a slogan and not a feeling. If you cannot, that is worth knowing, and it is not a verdict on the belief. The ayah's demand is simply that a claim have a shape somebody could examine.
studies.explainEasier: God watches over every person and what they do. So the ayah tells them to name the partners they claim. Either they are telling God something he does not know, or they are just using empty words.

studies.title: No Defender Against Him
studies.meaning: A short ayah in three clauses, moving from the present to what follows and then to a denial. There is something painful in this nearer life. What comes after it is harder. And there is nobody to shield them from it. The word for harder is unusual. It means more difficult to bear rather than more acute. Early scholars discuss what the present suffering refers to and record several readings, from defeat and loss to the condition of a person who has closed their own hearing.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among early scholars. The ayah follows the challenge to name what has been set up beside God, and completes it. Its closing word, for a defender or shield, appears again three ayat later. There it is applied to the messenger himself. The same protection is denied to two very different people within a few lines.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the root for splitting, used of hardship rather than of pain. What is described is a weight harder to carry rather than a sensation more acute, which is a deliberate distinction.
The participle from the verb to guard against something, the same root behind the word for mindfulness of God. It occurs twice in this surah and once elsewhere, and always inside a denial.

The adjective is a comparative meaning closer, not lower. Arabic names this life by its proximity rather than by any judgement on its quality, which the usual translation as worldly slightly obscures.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was a named relationship you could point at. If you were threatened, somebody stood between you and the threat. Everyone knew who that was for each person in a settlement. Saying a man had no shield at all described a condition people could picture exactly. It was the most exposed position anybody in that society could hold.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a shield used at the end of this ayah appears again three ayat later at 13:37. There it is applied to the messenger himself, inside a conditional sentence. Within a few lines the same protection is denied to two entirely different people. Once it comes as a consequence, and once as a warning about what would follow.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah refuses to postpone everything to a later date. Something is happening already. The classical readings of what that is vary enough to suggest it is not one obvious event. The comparative is then chosen with care. What comes is harder rather than sharper. And the closing clause removes the option people reach for first. That option is not escape but rescue by somebody stronger.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a shield, applied there to the messenger in a conditional warning.
Uses the identical phrase about having no defender against God, of earlier peoples.
Sets the same comparison between this life and the next, measured a different way.

studies.applyIt: Notice who you assume will step in if something goes badly wrong: a parent, an employer, a savings account, a person with influence. Name them honestly. Then hold the ayah's last clause beside that list, not as a threat but as a question about how much weight each of those names can actually take.
studies.explainEasier: They have pain in this life already. What comes after it is harder still. And there is nobody at all who can shield them from God.

studies.title: Its Food And Its Shade
studies.meaning: A description made almost entirely of one repeated word: perpetual. The rivers run beneath, and then two things are named as unending, food and shade. Early scholars note the choice. These are not gold or company or peace, but the two things a desert traveller runs out of. The closing sentence then names the other outcome in four words. A description of one destination is balanced against a very short statement about its opposite.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with early scholars recording disagreement about it. The word opening the description means a likeness or comparison. Early scholars take that seriously. What follows is offered as an approximation rather than a report. The same opening phrase occurs once more in the Quran, at 47:15, where the description after it is considerably longer.

keyTerms.note: The word for a parable or similitude. Its presence at the head of the description signals an approximation rather than a report, which early scholars take seriously when reading everything that follows it.
From a verb meaning to go on without interruption. It is applied to the food and to the shade together, and what it denies is not scarcity but the ending that everything in this world eventually has.
From the root for a heel, so the word names what comes along behind. This surah uses it three times, which makes it one of the chapter's own characteristic terms for a final result.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade in Arabia was a resource rather than a comfort. Travellers timed a day's stage by where shade would fall at noon, and a tree at a known point on a route was a landmark with a name. Food and shade were the two things that ran out on a journey and the two a host supplied on arrival. Naming those as perpetual answered the anxiety of the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening phrase of this ayah, naming the likeness of the Garden promised to the mindful, occurs twice in the Quran. Here it introduces a description two lines long; at 47:15 the identical phrase opens a description several times longer. One formula serves both a compressed account and an expanded one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The description is deliberately modest, and that modesty is itself a claim. What is promised is named in the language of relief from ordinary hardship, not in the language of splendour. And the word standing at the head of the sentence grants that this is a comparison. A reader is given something they can picture, while being told plainly that the picture is not the thing.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the identical phrase and gives a much longer description of the same place.
Describes the same destination earlier in the surah, naming company rather than provisions.
Extends the same imagery of shade and unfailing fruit at considerably greater length.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you actually run out of, rather than what you would like more of. Sleep, patience, quiet, money at the end of the month. The two things named here are the two that ran out on a desert road. Name yours honestly this week; it tells you what a promise of perpetual would mean to you.
studies.explainEasier: The Garden promised to those who are careful has rivers running under it. Its food never runs out. Its shade never goes away. That is what waits for them at the end.

studies.title: I Am Commanded To Worship
studies.meaning: Two reactions are reported side by side and neither is explained. Some of those given the earlier scripture rejoice at what has been revealed. Among the factions, some refuse to recognise part of it. The reply that follows addresses neither group. It states the speaker's own instruction in four clauses, naming worship, the refusal to associate anything, an invitation, and a return. Early scholars note that the reply narrows the ground rather than arguing over it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded. The word rendered as parties or factions is used across the Quran for coalitions of opponents. Early scholars read it here as covering groups from more than one community. The reply follows the pattern set a few ayat earlier at 13:30, where an objection is met with a first-person statement rather than a rebuttal.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a group bound by a common cause, used across the Quran of coalitions formed against a messenger. It names people by their alignment rather than by any belief they hold.
The verb for denying that you know something, the opposite of acknowledging it. What is described is a refusal to recognise part of what is presented, rather than an argument against the whole.
The verb for calling somebody towards you, the same one used for prayer. The speaker's task is named with a word that faces outward, and it is followed straight away by the word for his own return.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina held communities with older scriptures and long-standing learning. People inside them did not all react the same way to a new claim. Some crossed over. Some argued. Some took parts of it and refused the rest. All of it happened in public. Reporting two responses in one sentence describes a city where nobody could speak for a whole group.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for factions used here occurs ten times in the Quran. It is nearly always applied to coalitions formed against a messenger, not to any settled community. It names a group by what it has assembled against. That is why this ayah can use it of people drawn from more than one background at the same time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply answers a divided reception with an undivided statement. Rather than sorting the objectors, it restates what the speaker was instructed to do. Every clause of it is in the first person. That refusal to bargain over parts does something specific. A message accepted in fragments is treated as a different thing from the message. And nobody is condemned for the fragments they took.

crossReferences.why: Answers a different objection with the same technique, a first-person statement rather than a rebuttal.
Names the same partial reception directly, and puts it to the reader as a question.
Reports the same positive reception among people holding an earlier scripture.

studies.applyIt: Think about which parts of what you believe you actually act on and which you have quietly filed away. Everyone does this and it is rarely deliberate. Pick one filed item and take it out this week. The ayah does not attack anyone for it; it simply states what the whole instruction was.
studies.explainEasier: Some people who have the older books are glad about this message. Others refuse part of it. He is told to say that he was ordered to worship God alone, and that he calls people to him.

studies.title: Sent Down In Arabic
studies.meaning: The revelation is described in two words, a judgement and Arabic. Early scholars unpack that as decisive guidance delivered in a particular language. Then a conditional aimed at the messenger himself. Were you to follow their leanings after the knowledge that has reached you, you would have neither ally nor shield. Early scholars note how severe it is to address this to him. They read it as setting out that the message is not his to adjust.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classed as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among early scholars. The phrase naming the revelation as an Arabic judgement occurs only here. The conditional that follows belongs to a group of passages addressed to the messenger in the same form. They warn against giving ground. Early scholars read them as a lesson for the audience rather than as a hint that it might happen.

keyTerms.note: From the root for restraining and deciding, which also gives the words for wisdom and for a bridle. What it names is guidance that settles matters, so the noun carries the sense of ending disputes rather than starting them.

The adjective names the language, and its pairing with a word for judgement occurs only in this ayah. The Quran repeatedly notes the language of its own delivery, treating that as part of what is being described.

From a root meaning to fall or incline, the same one behind the word for air. Desires are pictured as a slope you slide down rather than as choices, which is why following them is described as a direction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic carried weight among its own speakers and very little beyond them. Persian, Greek and Syriac carried the empires. They carried the older scriptures around Arabia too. Calling a revelation Arabic was a claim about a language outsiders had dismissed. It was also a claim about people who had never had a scripture in their own speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase naming this revelation as an Arabic judgement occurs only in this ayah. The Quran refers to the language of its own delivery a number of times elsewhere. It always does so in the same way. It is a fact about how the message arrives, not a claim that the language itself is better than any other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sending the warning to the messenger does real work. If the man who delivers a message would have no cover for changing it, then the message is plainly not his to change. Everyone listening learns that in the strongest form there is. Putting judgement next to language also says something modest. What settles matters arrives in one tongue, at one time, to one people.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a shield three ayat earlier, applied to a very different group.
Gives the same conditional warning to the messenger about following their desires.
Names the language of the revelation and gives a reason for it directly.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you soften something true because of who is listening. Not tact, which is a courtesy, but the version that removes what the other person would dislike. Pick one such conversation this week and say the unsoftened sentence kindly. The difficulty of doing it is what this ayah is describing.
studies.explainEasier: God sent this down as a clear judgement in Arabic. The Prophet is told that if he follows what they want, after what he now knows, no one at all will protect him from God.

studies.title: He Erases And Confirms
studies.meaning: Three statements about messengers come first, then one about writing. Earlier messengers had wives and children. That answers an objection without ever stating it. No messenger brought a sign except by God's permission, so the power was never his. Every set term has a writing. Then the second ayah: God erases what He wills and fixes what He wills. With Him is the source of the Book. Early scholars differ widely over what is erased. They record the range rather than settle it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement about that. The first statement answers a reported objection: a man with a household could not be a messenger. The Quran states that objection elsewhere in similar words. The second ayah drew a great deal of classical discussion. Readings range from records of deeds, to instructions later replaced, to the length of a lifespan.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word meaning one of a pair. Some people assumed a prophet must stand outside ordinary life. Naming wives of earlier messengers answers that, and it answers by reporting rather than by arguing.
The verb for rubbing something off a surface. It is used of writing taken off a tablet. The word assumes something written, which is why the end of the ayah names a book rather than a decision.
The Arabic says the mother of the Book. Arabic uses the word for a mother to mean an origin or a chief thing. So the phrase names a master copy, not any family relation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: People wrote on materials made to be used again. Wooden boards were whitewashed, written on, then washed clean. Leather and parchment were scraped and used a second time. Erasing and fixing were two ordinary stages of one craft. Any scribe would have heard the pair as a picture of work in progress. He would not have heard it as indecision.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase that closes the second ayah names the source of the Book. It occurs three times in the Quran: here, at 3:7 and at 43:4. Each time it ends a passage about what is fixed and what is open to reading. Each time it names something held with God, not in anybody's hands.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat work together, and they work carefully. The first says messengers were ordinary and dependent. They had households, and they had no power over signs. The second puts all the deciding somewhere else, in a book that is written and edited. Between them, anything that might be credited to the man delivering the message is moved away from him. The surah has been doing that since its opening line.

crossReferences.why: Records the objection this ayah answers, that a messenger should not live an ordinary life.
Uses the same phrase for the source of the Book, in a passage about clear and unclear ayat.
Makes the same point about signs, that the whole matter belongs to God alone.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much you expect of people you admire. Notice how quickly plainness in them looks like a reason to doubt them. The first sentence here names households and children as plain facts about prophets. Give one person you look up to permission this week to be tired, wrong, or busy with something small.
studies.explainEasier: God says that the prophets before were normal people. They had wives and children. They could only show a sign if God let them. God can wipe out what He wants and keep what He wants. The first book is with Him.

studies.title: Yours To Tell, Ours To Reckon
studies.meaning: The sentence is built as a division of labour. Whether We show you some of what We promise them, or take you first, the two tasks stay the same. Yours is the delivering. Ours is the reckoning. The conditional is unusual, because both branches end in the same place. So nothing turns on which one happens. Early scholars point to the two possessives. They carry the whole meaning: two jobs handed out, and only one of them to the man addressed.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, and disagreement is recorded. The ayah belongs to a group of passages that address the messenger about outcomes he might not live to see. Early scholars read it as answering an unspoken worry rather than a stated objection. Similar sentences appear in several surahs. Each one separates the task of conveying from the task of judging.

keyTerms.note: A causative of the verb to see, with an emphatic ending. The first branch of the conditional is about witnessing rather than about achieving. What he might or might not be given is a sight.
The verb for collecting a payment in full, used across the Quran for death. Placing it as the alternative to seeing an outcome treats dying as simply the other branch, with no extra weight attached.
From the verb to reach a destination, so the noun names getting a message all the way to its hearer. It says nothing about what happens after arrival. That silence is the whole point of the division.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger in Arabia carried words and was not answerable for them. He crossed to another tribe, delivered what he had been given, and came back. What the hearers did about it lay between them and whoever had sent him. The role was well defined and well understood. This ayah uses its exact words to describe a much larger job.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that only the conveying is upon you occurs three times in the Quran: here, at 3:20 and at 16:82. Each time it closes an exchange rather than opening one. Each time the sentence around it makes the same split: delivery on one side, and everything after delivery on the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah releases a person from responsibility for a result. It does so in a passage about opponents who have not been won over. That is a specific comfort and also a specific limit. It treats the two possible futures as equal. Quietly, that says seeing the outcome of your work was never part of the assignment.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about the duty being only to convey, at the close of an argument.
Gives almost the same conditional about being shown some of it or being taken first.
Names the same office earlier in the surah, describing the messenger as only a warner.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you are carrying that is not yours to settle: someone else's decision, a change at work, how a relative treats you. Write out, in two short lines, what your part is and what is not. Then do only your part this week. Notice how much room that leaves.
studies.explainEasier: God tells his messenger that his job is only to pass the message on. God will do the judging. It does not matter if the messenger sees how it all ends, or dies before that.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Reduced At Its Edges
studies.meaning: The ayah asks about something people can see, and the picture is territorial. We come to the land and cut it back from its outer parts. Early scholars divide over what this means. Some read it as land lost by opponents. Some read it as the death of scholars and notable people. Some read it as the earth simply wearing away. Two short clauses then close the ayah. God judges, and nothing comes behind His judgement to turn it over. The last phrase names how fast the reckoning is.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement. The same wording occurs once more in the Quran, at 21:44, in a similar setting. The ayah asks whether people have seen something, which implies a process already visible at the time. The classical readings differ, and that reflects real uncertainty about what the first listeners were being shown.

keyTerms.note: The verb for making something less, used of measures and of numbers. It describes subtraction rather than destruction. What the ayah names is a steady lessening, not any single disaster.
The plural of a word for a limb or an outer point. It can mean the borders of a territory or the ends of a thing. The scholars' disagreement turns largely on which sense is meant.
From the root for a heel, so the word names somebody coming up behind to overturn what was done. It belongs to the language of judgement, where an appeal follows a decision.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Land in Arabia was held at its margins. Grazing rights, wells and control of routes were fought over at the edges of a tribe's range. A territory shrank by losing its outer places one at a time, not by being taken whole. Anybody who moved animals with the seasons understood a range shrinking from the rim inwards. They had watched it happen.
studies.didYouKnow: This sentence appears twice in the Quran, here and at 21:44, in nearly identical words. Both times it is a question about something people should already have noticed. The classical scholars offer several readings of what is being reduced. They record them all rather than choosing, which is unusual for a phrase repeated so exactly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah points at a process rather than an event, and asks whether it has been noticed. That is a different kind of evidence from a sign. It is gradual, already under way, and easy to live inside without noticing at all. The closing clauses then call it judgement in progress, and say that nothing follows it to overturn it. That makes the slow thing the serious one.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same sentence in almost identical words, inside a similar warning.
Names the same kind of ongoing calamity earlier in the surah, striking near their homes.
States the same claim that judgement belongs to God and to nobody called upon beside Him.

studies.applyIt: Think about what has been shrinking at the edges of your life rather than collapsing in the middle: energy, a group of friends, the hours you get to yourself. Nothing has gone wrong, so nothing has asked for attention. Name one such edge today and decide whether you mind. That is the ayah's question, in miniature.
studies.explainEasier: God asks if people notice the land getting smaller at its edges, bit by bit. God is the one doing it. When God decides something, no one can come after Him and change it back.

studies.title: The Whole Plan Is His
studies.meaning: A short ayah with a large reversal inside it. Those before them planned, and then the sentence takes the word back. All of the planning belongs to God. Early scholars note the wording. It does not say His plan is better; it says the whole of it is His, and that is a stronger claim. Then comes a statement about knowing what every soul earns. The ayah closes by promising that those who deny will learn whose the final outcome is.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement. The ayah sits in the last few lines of the chapter. Those lines gather several of its threads: the pattern of earlier peoples, the knowledge of what is hidden, and the final outcome. The word for outcome used at the end appears three times in this surah. Scholars note it as one of the surah's own terms.

keyTerms.note: The verb for arranging something the other side cannot see. It is used first of people and then of God inside one sentence. Early scholars explain that as answering a hidden plan in kind, not as deception.
One word turns the sentence from a comparison into a claim about ownership. It does not say His planning is better. It says the whole category is His, which leaves nothing standing outside it.

An idiom for the final result, built on the word for what follows behind. The phrase occurs three times in the Quran, and all three are in this surah. That makes it one of the surah's own expressions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Planning was often the only weapon a smaller party had. An ambush at a well, a false report sent ahead, an alliance arranged quietly before a dispute broke: these decided outcomes more often than numbers did. Everyone knew that the unseen half of a conflict mattered most. That is why a claim about who owns the planning would have landed hard.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the final outcome used at the end of this ayah occurs three times in the Quran. All three are in this surah, at 13:22, at 13:24 and here. The first two describe what the patient receive. This one leaves the question open, and says that those who deny will find out for themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reversal in the first line is the whole ayah. Saying that all planning belongs to God is not a claim that His scheme will beat other schemes. That would leave the other schemes real and merely weaker. It says the category itself is His, so a hidden plan is not a second thing running alongside. The clause about knowledge then closes the gap from the other side.

crossReferences.why: Describes a specific plot answered in kind, using the same verb of both parties.
States the same principle at its largest scale, that no scheme escapes the reckoning.
Uses the same phrase for the final outcome, applied there to those who were patient.

studies.applyIt: Think of a situation where you suspect something is being arranged without you. The ayah does not tell you what it is, and it does not promise you a good result. It says the whole business of hidden arranging is not a place where you are alone. Act on what you can see this week, and stop rehearsing what you cannot.
studies.explainEasier: People before them made secret plans. But God is the one who really plans everything. He knows what every person is doing and earning. In the end, those who say no to God will see who really wins.

studies.title: God Is Witness Enough
studies.meaning: The surah closes on the flattest possible denial: he is not a messenger at all. The reply calls witnesses. The first is God, described as sufficient, which settles the matter on its own. A second is then added: whoever has knowledge of the Book. Early scholars divide over who that names. Some say God under another description, some say people holding earlier scripture, and some say those who know the revelation being given. The surah ends without settling it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, and early scholars record disagreement. The denial reported here is the simplest form of the objection the surah has been answering since its first ayah. The reply is correspondingly short. The disagreement over the second witness is an old one. The classical commentaries set the readings side by side and prefer none of them.

keyTerms.note: The verb for something being adequate to a need, with no comparison implied. Its use here means the testimony closes the matter. It does not mean the testimony outweighs whatever the other side might bring.
From the verb for being present and seeing. Arabic builds testimony out of presence, so a witness is somebody who was there. That is why the same word can also name one who dies for a cause.
The phrase occurs only in this ayah. It names nobody exactly, which is why the early scholars divide over it. The surah closes on a description rather than on a name.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the whole legal system. There were no records, so a claim stood or fell on who would appear and say what they had seen. The standing of a witness mattered as much as their words. Naming a witness was the ordinary way of closing an argument, and everybody listening knew exactly what the move meant.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the second witness, whoever has knowledge of the Book, occurs only in this ayah in the whole Quran. The classical scholars record several readings of it and do not settle the question. So the surah closes on a description that has never been finally tied to any one party.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply answers a denial of office by calling a witness rather than by offering proof. That fits the whole approach of this surah. It has spent forty ayat pointing at things a person can already see, and refusing to produce the sign that was demanded. Ending on a witness rather than on a demonstration is consistent with that. The closing ambiguity leaves a reader still looking.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah with the claim this denial answers, that the revelation is the truth.
Uses the same formula about God being sufficient as a witness between two parties.
Adds the testimony of the angels to God's own, in a similar reply to the same denial.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your energy goes into being believed by people who have already decided. The reply here is one sentence long, and it names a witness rather than making a case. Pick one argument you keep re-fighting and stop making the case in it. Say what is true once, and let it stand.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said he was not sent by God at all. The answer given is short. God is enough as a witness that he was. So is anyone who really knows the Book.
